Zion National Park
Zion National Park  is a United States National Park located in the southern Utah regions of Dixie and Canyon Country. The park protects the incredible rock formations and high sandstone cliffs within its boundaries and is a favorite spot for hiking, backpacking, canyoneering and climbing. In fact, Zion has some of the most spectacular trails in the National Park System. Visitors to Zion walk on the canyon floor and look up, rather than looking down from the rim as in many parks. In addition to the magnificent monoliths and cliffs, the park is known for its desert landscape of sandstone canyons, mesas, and high plateaus.
Mormon pioneer Issac Behunin built the first log cabin in Zion Canyon in 1863, near the location of the current Zion Lodge. Behunin Canyon, a technical slot canyon, was named after him. During the remainder of the century, small communities and homesteads in the area struggled to survive. Pioneers gave the canyon the name "Zion", a Hebrew word meaning safety, or a place of refuge. Despite the name, the canyon offered little arable land, poor soil, and catastrophic flooding, making agriculture a risky venture. By the first decade of the 20th century, the scenic qualities of southern Utah, and Zion Canyon in particular, had been recognized as a potential destination for tourism. In 1909, a presidential executive order designated Mukuntuweap National Monument. The new monument was, however, virtually inaccessible to visitors, since the existing roads were in poor condition and the closest railhead was a hundred miles away. The monument's name was changed to Zion National Monument in 1918, and in 1919 the monument was expanded and designated a national park. Visitation to the new national park increased steadily during the 1920s, and in 1930, the newly completed Zion-Mt Carmel Highway allowed motorists to travel through the park to Mount Carmel Junction, then on to Bryce Canyon and the Grand Canyon. This highway was one of the greatest engineering feats of modern times, requiring the construction of a 5,613-foot tunnel, the Zion-Mt. Carmel Tunnel, to negotiate the vertical sandstone cliffs of Zion. The switchbacks leading up to the tunnel proved to be an even greater task to accomplish. The Kolob Canyons section, near Cedar City was established as a National Monument in 1937 and added to Zion National Park in 1956.
Flora and fauna
Although Zion is in an arid desert climate, the park has almost nine-hundred native species of plants, seventy-five species of mammals, two-hundred-ninety species of birds including the recent addition of the California Condor, forty-four species of reptiles and amphibians and eight native fish.
Mammals commonly found within the park's borders include bats, jack rabbits, chipmunks, squirrels, gophers, kangaroo rats, beavers, mice, porcupines, coyotes, gray fox, ringtails, skunks, mule deer and the rarely seen mountain lions. Peregrine falcons, rattlesnakes and numerous lizards are also species that visitors may recognize.
There is a wide variety of plant life in the park, seeing that the unique geology has created diverse environments such as deserts, canyons, slickrock, hanging gardens, riparian, and high plateaus. There are many beautiful wildflowers, including the Sacrad Datura, which is common in Zion and is often found along the Zion-Mt. Carmel Highway and on the canyon floor in Zion Canyon.
Weather in the park varies greatly with elevation, and even at the same elevation may differ by over 30°F between day and night. During the spring the weather is very unpredictable, with stormy, wet days common, although warm, sunny weather may occur too. Precipitation peaks in March. Summer days are hot (95-110°F), but overnight lows are usually comfortable (65-70°F). Afternoon thunderstorms are common from mid-July through mid-September, making flash floods (if hiking in one) in the canyons a danger. Autumn days are usually clear and mild with cool nights. Winter storms bring rain or light snow to Zion Canyon, but heavier snow to the higher elevations such as the east side of the park, Kolob Terrace and Kolob Canyons. Clear days may become quite warm, reaching 60°F; nights are often in the 20s and 30s. Winter storms can last several days and cause roads to be icy, but the Zion-Mt. Carmel Highway is owned by the park and the NPS keeps it in excellent condition even in the winter.
There are sections of the park that are not connected by road; the Kolob Canyons area is in the park's northern area and offers interesting canyon views and hiking. The remote Kolob Terrace offers an uncrowded and scenic drive, spectacular slot canyons and hiking. The highly photographed "Subway" is found in this section of the park. The more popular (and more crowded) Zion Canyon area is in the southern portion of the park and contains many of the park's most famous scenic wonders such as Angels Landing and the Great White Throne. The Zion-Mt. Carmel Highway runs from the south entrance of the park to the east entrance featuring magnificent landmarks and hiking along the way such as East Temple, Checkerboard Mesa and the Great Arch. The Zion Narrows and Orderville Canyon, two of the parks most popular canyons begin on the east rim of the park and end in Zion Canyon.
Zion Canyon, the most popular section of the park, is accessed by taking SR-9 from the east or the west.
From the west: I-15 passes west of Zion and connects with SR-9 just north of St. George. From there SR-9 travels through the towns of Hurricane, Virgin, and Springdale before entering Zion Canyon.
From the east: US-89 passes east of Zion and connects with SR-9 (The Zion-Mt. Carmel Highway) at Mount Carmel Junction. From there SR-9 travels through the park's east Entrance and into the Zion-Mt. Carmel Tunnel before descending into Zion Canyon.
The Kolob Terrace road is accessed off SR-9 in the town of Virgin, west of Zion. The Kolob Canyons entrance is accessible from I-15, exit 40, near Cedar City.
NOTE: Visitors driving RVs, pulling trailers, or with any vehicle that is over 7'10" wide or over 11'4" tall should be aware that due to the small size of the tunnel an escort is required to pass through the Zion-Mt. Carmel Tunnel; the fee for this escort is $15, valid for a round-trip. Most RVs, buses, trailers, 5th wheels, and some camper shells require an escort. Escorts are at the tunnel from 8AM-8PM during the busy season and arranged at the entrance gate in the winter. Semi-tractor trailers are not permitted in the park.
The Zion Canyon Scenic Drive is accessible only by the Zion Canyon Shuttle the majority of the year, but from November until the end of March, private vehicles are allowed to drive into the canyon.
St. George is the closest city with commercial airline service. St. George opened the new, larger St. George Municipal Airport  in January 2011, which services the area with flights from Salt Lake City on Delta Connection and from Los Angeles on United Express. Both routes are operated by SkyWest. Flying into Cedar City (30 miles north of Zion National Park) from Salt Lake City on SkyWest is an additional option.
The second closest major airport is in Salt Lake City , about a five hour drive on I-15.
There is no public transportation into the park. Tour buses can be arranged through travel agencies, and Greyhound buses visit the cities of Salt Lake City, Cedar City, St. George, plus Las Vegas in Nevada. For Utah Greyhound information call +1 435

claim.title: L55_N11703: A Conditional Colorado Jurisdiction/Contact–Citation Frame with a Narrow Negative Pole and Limited Generalization
claim.lede: For neuron L55_N11703, strong positive responses appear in Colorado-framed jurisdiction/name contexts—especially administrative, contact, and citation strings—while a few formatted other-jurisdiction strings are negative, but this is sparse/selected evidence with limited generalization and no established broad non-Colorado suppression. The main qualification is that the neuron may instead track a generic administrative/contact/citation format rather than a Colorado-specific frame.

pattern.text: For L55_N11703, the best-supported response is a conditional Colorado jurisdiction/name frame keyed by the causal prefix through the scored token—explicit Colorado, C.R.S., Denver/Boulder/Longmont, or Colorado institutions usually score high (e.g., 306.0 at a space in a C.R.S. citation, 322.0 in a Denver contact, 314.0 for Longmont–720, and blind 286 versus target 306)—often on a space or adjacent ordinary token, though explicit Colorado is not sufficient (84/87 P1 and 31/32 P5 positive, with negative Colorado-list/Plateau cases and 68446290), and the corpus is mostly near zero (median −0.048; 99.2% in −2…2). The observed negative pole is narrow: formatted other-jurisdiction administrative/contact/citation strings score low (Qinghai −46.75; North Dakota Game and Fish −39.25; blind “ (” −45.0), whereas a non-Colorado country control is −0.07 and generic phone/section strings are not negative (+3.69/+26.88), so broad non-Colorado place-name or format-alone suppression is rejected. These are measured but sparse/selected observations; the route accuracy (53.3% versus 13.3%, n=15 saved test split, including a p2→n2 counterexample) is split-limited, and the negative pole remains a hypothesis outside the exemplified administrative/citation/grant blocks.

strength.text: Strong positive responses occur in Colorado-framed prefixes (Denver contact 322; Longmont contact 314; C.R.S. citation 306; blind maximum 286 vs target 306), and at aligned scored spaces within the replacement span of `Contact:` the Longmont frame scored product 304 (gate 17.875, up 17.0) versus Fort Collins 217 (gate 16.75, up 12.9375), with the −87.0 change decomposing into −16.84 gate and −70.33 up; sampled gate/up signs are mostly +/+ in positive bins and +/- in negative bins. The negative pole is narrow and observed on other-jurisdiction administrative strings (ND Game and Fish −39.25; Qinghai −46.75; blind minimum −45 vs target −44.5), while generic controls are weak or positive (non-Colorado country −0.07; generic phone +3.69; generic section +26.88) and the equal-quota spectrum is mostly near zero (median −0.048) with no-visible-cue positions at both tails. Route prediction reached 53.3% versus 13.3% baseline only on the saved test split (n=15), with an atlas-a14 predicted-p2/actual-n2 counterexample, so the Colorado frame is supported but broad non-Colorado suppression and generalization remain limited hypotheses.

mechanism.text: At the aligned scored space in the `Contact: {slot}.` template (same-template, same-position, not an other-jurisdiction control), the native SiLU(gate)×up product fell from 304.0 for Longmont, CO (gate 17.875, up 17.0) to 217.0 for Fort Collins, CO (gate 16.75, up 12.9375), decomposed as −16.84 from gate and −70.33 from up (0.172 residual), so the drop is mostly `up`. Ablating L55_N11703 across 80 cases gave median KL 0.00342 versus 0.000227 for same-position controls, strongest on strong-positive cases (0.362 vs 0.000279), smaller on strong-negative (0.00622 vs 0.000469) and medium (0.00262 vs 0.000316), near control for weak cases (0.000245 vs 0.000081), and mixed on controlled Colorado contact/URL probes. The 40 saved RelP atlas graphs show large positive incoming flow for Colorado/local-contact prefixes (graph-1 activation 332; graph-3 314) and negative flow for “Qinghai” (graph-2 −46.5), but these are attributional route observations using separate-sample readers with no same-position intervention controls, so downstream causality is supported but not uniform.

open_questions.text: The most important unresolved alternative is that L55_N11703 tracks a generic administrative/contact/citation format rather than a Colorado/jurisdiction frame: the negative pole is narrow (N2 33/35 and N4 17/17 negative, but Montana 406 and Utah 801 civic contacts are positive and the Basque Club 775/435 contact is a boundary case), and while a North Dakota Game and Fish administrative/phone prefix is strongly negative (−39.25), generic phone and section strings are not (+3.69 and +26.88). A same-template, same-position sweep crossing Colorado and other-jurisdiction contact/citation/grant strings, with measured ablations against same-position controls, could distinguish these accounts; current controlled Colorado contact/URL probes were mixed (median KL 0.150 vs 0.000268 controls), so the jurisdiction-specific reading remains a hypothesis rather than a settled causal finding.

ablation.summary: Across 80 completed ablations, L55_N11703 ablation yielded an overall median KL of 0.00342 versus 0.000227 for same-position controls, with the strongest effect on strong-positive cases (median KL 0.362 vs 0.000279) and smaller elevated effects on strong-negative (0.00622 vs 0.000469) and medium cases (0.00262 vs 0.000316); weak cases sat near control (0.000245 vs 0.000081). The key qualification is nonuniformity: controlled Colorado contact/URL probes were mixed, large for “Denver, CO” and “Longmont” but near zero for a generic contact URL. Thus the measured activation is causally implicated in some Colorado-framed contexts, but the evidence does not show a uniform effect across all frozen-claim categories.

anatomy.summary: At the aligned scored space within the replacement span of the `Contact: {slot}.` template, the Longmont, CO frame measured gate 17.875, up 17.0, and product 304.0, while the Fort Collins, CO frame measured gate 16.75, up 12.9375, and product 217.0; the native product change of −87.0 is reconstructed as −16.84 from the gate term and −70.33 from the up term, with a 0.172 residual. This is a same-template, same-position comparison of two Colorado contact frames, not an other-jurisdiction negative control, and the recorded quantities are rounded.

circuit.summary: Across the 40 saved atlas graphs, signed root-directed RelP attributions show large positive incoming flow at scored spaces when the causal prefix carries a Colorado/local-contact frame (graph-1 activation 332 with a Denver/Boulder phone prefix; graph-3 activation 314 with “Longmont”) and negative flow for an other-jurisdiction administrative prefix (graph-2 activation −46.5 with “Qinghai”). The nominated readers are directionally compatible but are separate sample correlates—L14_N489 (+1.05 on “ Kids”), L62_N21256 (+30.6 on “www”), and L59_N9433 (+17.6 on “ at”)—while the method detaches intervening MLP outputs. No ablation or same-position control is reported here, so these remain attributional route observations rather than measured causal interventions.

criticism.summary: The criticism checks largely narrow rather than overturn the frozen account: the broad non-Colorado place-name negative rule is rejected (P1 84/87 positive, with California/Texas/Utah/New Mexico near neutral and Bolivia/Nepal rows positive), and explicit Colorado is usually positive but not sufficient (P1 84/87; P5 31/32, with negative Colorado-list/Plateau cases and 68446290). The other-jurisdiction negative pole is supported only after narrowing to formal administrative/citation/grant blocks: N2 is 33/35 negative and N4 17/17, but Montana 406 and Utah 801 civic contacts are positive and the Basque Club 775/435 contact is a boundary case. Substantive qualifications remain: P2’s citation effect is construction-specific with a tiny sample, mixed-prefix suppression is local to the other-jurisdiction token rather than global, and several follow-up or corpus results are exploratory, reused, cut-context, or not held out.

custom.summary: The custom section supports the frozen Colorado/jurisdiction frame: explicit Colorado naming, C.R.S. citation framing, and Colorado contact/URL context yield large positive activations (for example 157.0, 304.0, and 314.0 at scored positions), while matched generic strings remain weak or near zero. The key qualification is that the negative pole is narrow: a North Dakota Game and Fish administrative/phone string is strongly negative (-39.25), and an explicit North Dakota name is negative (-7.75), but generic phone and section strings are not negative (+3.69 and +26.88) and the non-Colorado country control is weak (-0.07). These are measured observations from the supplied custom cases and do not support broad non-Colorado place-name or format-alone negative rules.

family.summary: The family probes produced high target products (274, 260, 235, 122) on spaces, “ the,” and “ Colorado” within Colorado statutory, local-media/contact, statehood, and contrastive administrative contexts, consistent with the frozen Colorado named-entity/jurisdiction frame. The key qualification is family:4: its 122 falls on the explicit token “ Colorado” after other-jurisdiction administrative strings, so it does not measure a negative response on those identifiers or show suppression of the edited span or suffix. No family case here supplies a strong negative-pole score, and these are scored-position observations rather than ablations.

search.summary: In the search section, the measured response is strongly positive on Colorado-framed prefixes—Colorado contact/address, C.R.S. citation, Colorado names, university science, and statehood cases score 238–322 at the scored token—while the included other-jurisdiction Qinghai administrative string scores −46.75. The positives often land on a space, function word, or adjacent ordinary token inside the Colorado frame, so the observed pattern is consistent with a frame-level Colorado detector rather than a fixed token class, and the negative is an observed counterexample to broad non-Colorado suppression rather than evidence for it. The main qualification is sparse, selected evidence: corpus activations are mostly near zero (median −0.048) with a rare high positive tail, and the narrow other-jurisdiction negative pole remains a hypothesis outside the exemplified administrative strings.

spectrum.summary: Across 100M tokens the neuron is sharply heavy-tailed and centered slightly below zero: median −0.048, with 99% of positions between −0.777 and 1.211, about 99.2% in the −2…2 bin, and tails extending to −44.5 and 306. The upper tail is more populated, and labeled high-positive bins are dominated by P1/P5 (with some P3/P4 and a few no-visible-cue positions), whereas negative-tail bins mix N2/N4 with many no-visible-cue positions. The key qualification is that the spectrum is an equal-quota, bin-balanced sample rather than a random corpus sample, and the extremes include no-visible-cue counterexamples (e.g., a −44.5 space in Qinghai geographic text versus a +306 space in a Colorado C.R.S. citation frame).

tests.summary: On the saved test split (n=15; 25 train), route prediction reached 53.3% accuracy versus a 13.3% baseline, but this result is limited to that split and is not a general estimate. Blind tests of the frozen explanation tracked both extrema: the maximum achieved 286 versus a target of 306 at a space in a Colorado Department of Education C.R.S. citation prefix, and the minimum achieved -45 versus a target of -44.5 at “ (” in a North Dakota Game and Fish contact string. These are individual extrema and the supplied atlas-a14 route case is a counterexample (predicted p2, actual n2), so the aggregate accuracy and extrema should be read as measured test evidence rather than broad validation.

details.result: The broad place-name account fails. The frozen P1 family was 84/87 positive, yet its three misses were Colorado-list or Colorado-plateau contexts scored negative (20801103, 64969991, 51093128). Controls put California, Texas, Utah, New Mexico and a country near neutral, with Nevada -7.34, North Dakota -7.75, and Qinghai -4.65, not uniformly strong. Non-Colorado positives remain, so the broad negative rule is rejected rather than confirmed.

criticism:original-2.label: Criticism · original-2
criticism:original-2.text: Explicit Colorado name is sufficient for positivity.

details.result: Explicit Colorado is usually positive but not sufficient. P1 is 84/87 positive, and P5 is 31/32, yet P1 has negative Colorado-list and Colorado-Plateau cases, and P5 includes 68446290, where a University of Colorado list precedes a North Dakota anchor and the measured value is -20.375. The rule should be narrowed by competing other-jurisdiction administrative framing and list context, not treated as a context-free Colorado keyword detector.

criticism:original-3.label: Criticism · original-3
criticism:original-3.text: N2 catches all other-jurisdiction contact strings.

details.result: N2 is strong but not jurisdiction-general. It is 33/35 negative and N4 is 17/17 negative, mostly on North Dakota 701, N.D.C.C., Nevada 775, Utah 435, and Qinghai grants. However, 56828588 (Montana 406 contact) and 53716305 (Utah foot clinics 801) are measured positive. These are ordinary local institutional/contact contexts, so N2 should be narrowed to formatted administrative/citation/grant blocks, leaving other-jurisdiction clinic or civic contacts as unresolved counterexamples.

criticism:original-4.label: Criticism · original-4
criticism:original-4.text: Generic citation, digit or punctuation formatting.

details.result: The generic-citation rival fails. P2 is only 3/3 positive, but its controls separate frames: C.R.S. prefix 280, C.R.S. suffix 79.5 and section-symbol form 304, while bare digits peak at 20 and a grant number is -0.957. N.D.C.C. § 28-33-02 is -28 and the Qinghai grant block is -38.25. Citation punctuation alone is therefore rejected; Colorado statutory material is doing the work, though P2's tiny sample limits generalization.

criticism:r1-i1.text: Follow-up round 1: In the three P1 misses (20801103, 64969991, 51093128), is an explicit 'Colorado' name actually present in the causal prefix before the marked position, or was the positive cue only a Colorado-adjacent token, nickname, regional list, or continuation after the anchor?

details.result:
Rival prediction is supported, so the no-explicit-Colorado hypothesis is rejected. In spectrum-20801103 the anchored token is a ')' in a 928 phone contact (activation -22.375), and the causal prefix already contains the literal state-list token 'Colorado' before that anchor. In spectrum-64969991 the anchored token is ' p' in a Montana/USDA citation page count (activation -16.5), and the prefix contains 'Boulder, CO' and 'University Press of Colorado' before that anchor. In spectrum-51093128 the anchored token is the space before '11th century' (activation -8.25), and the prefix contains 'Colorado Plateau' before that anchor. Thus these P1 misses are not explained by absence of explicit Colorado or by Colorado only after the anchor; explicit Colorado is present in the causal prefix in all three and still negative in list, other-jurisdiction administrative/citation, or plateau contexts. The supplied positive search-1-P1-0 (activation 195.0 at 'at') confirms explicit Colorado can be positive, but it does not make P1 a sufficient context-free rule. P1 must be narrowed by competing list/other-jurisdiction/administrative context.
Suggested revision: Refine P1 so that explicit 'Colorado' in the causal prefix is necessary but not sufficient: exclude cases where the anchor is inside another jurisdiction's contact/citation/admin string or where Colorado appears only as one item in a multi-state regional list or as a plateau/geologic term. Treat spectrum-20801103, spectrum-64969991, and spectrum-51093128 as counterexamples requiring that narrowing.
Evidence: spectrum-20801103, spectrum-64969991, spectrum-51093128, search-1-P1-0

criticism:r1-i2.label: Criticism · r1-i2
criticism:r1-i2.text: Follow-up round 1: Does 68446290's negative value arise from a competing other-jurisdiction administrative anchor in the causal prefix, rather than from the Colorado university/list material itself?

details.result:
The supplied 68446290 trace does not support the administrative-identifier version. Its Colorado university/list tokens are strongly positive (University of Colorado 191, '(' 222, 'B' 241, 'oulder' 50.25, later 'Colorado' 64.5), while the negative is localized at the later ' Dakota' in 'University of North Dakota' (-20.375; following '.' -16.25, 'Grand' -21.625). That is a competing other-jurisdiction named-entity/institutional cue, not the formatted phone/citation/grant pattern in search-1-N2-15 and search-2-N2-14, where the N2 block peaks at -40.75 on '(' in a North Dakota Department of Agriculture phone/N.D.C.C. string. Comparable Colorado P5 strings without a later North Dakota institution remain positive: search-1-P5-1 peaks 186 at ' Colorado' after 'and', and search-2-P5-1 peaks 227 at ' Colorado' after 'of'. Thus the rival that the Colorado/technical list itself causes the negative is weakened; the hypothesis survives only narrowed: a later competing other-jurisdiction institution/place, not specifically an administrative/citation string, explains 68446290. Because the excerpt is cut_left, I cannot exclude an omitted earlier cue, and these P5/N2 comparisons are reused or generated evidence, not held-out validation.
Suggested revision: Refine P5/N2 for the next round: keep Colorado higher-education/list frames positive when the causal prefix remains Colorado-framed, but add a narrow exception for a later competing other-jurisdiction institutional/place named entity in the same prefix (e.g., 'University of North Dakota'/'North Dakota') that can carry the negative at that later anchor. Do not generalize this to non-Colorado place names alone; require a competing institutional/place frame and test it on held-out contexts.
Evidence: spectrum-68446290, search-1-N2-15, search-2-N2-14, search-1-P5-1, search-2-P5-1

criticism:r1-i3.label: Criticism · r1-i3
criticism:r1-i3.text: Follow-up round 1: Are the positive N2 counterexamples 56828588 and 53716305 outside N2's scope because the other-jurisdiction contact/citation is not a formatted administrative identifier in the causal prefix, or because the jurisdiction cue occurs after the anchor?

details.result:
Mixed and not a survival of the stated working hypothesis. In the supplied token spans, both positive anchors follow other-jurisdiction contact material, so the 'jurisdiction cue after the anchor' explanation does not hold. spectrum-56828588 peaks at +6.65625 on the later 'Powder' (peak_index 512), after the 406-698-4720 Montana/NWF contact block. spectrum-53716305 peaks at +4.78125 on the '0' in Springville (801), after 'Clinics of Utah' and prior 801 phone blocks. The surviving distinction is format/type, not prefix position: the positives are ordinary civic/clinic phone contacts, while the strong negative N2 cases are formal administrative/legal/citation blocks: -44.0 at '(' in the North Dakota Department of Agriculture (701) block (spectrum-32442428), -45.0 at '(' before (701) in the North Dakota Game and Fish/N.D.C.C. example (blind-negative-0), and -43.0 at '3' in 775-738-9957 Elko Basque Club contact (spectrum-13854828). The Basque Club case shows N2 is not simply 'ordinary civic contacts are positive', so ordinary clinic/civic contact remains unresolved. Also, both excerpts are cut_left, so omitted earlier context limits full-context claims.
Suggested revision: Narrow N2 to formal other-jurisdiction administrative, legal, citation, or grant blocks in the causal prefix, with anchor-local punctuation/digit evidence, and do not treat ordinary clinic/civic contact pages as covered unless the anchor is on a formal administrative/citation string. Treat spectrum-56828588 and spectrum-53716305 as unresolved ordinary-contact/civic-contact exceptions rather than as support for a broad 'any other-jurisdiction contact string' rule; keep spectrum-13854828 as a boundary case showing that some ordinary civic contact blocks can still be negative.
Evidence: spectrum-56828588, spectrum-53716305, spectrum-32442428, spectrum-13854828, blind-negative-0

criticism:r1-i4.label: Criticism · r1-i4
criticism:r1-i4.text: Follow-up round 1: Is P2's positive effect specific to the Colorado statutory frame, or does the phrase 'per statutory reference in section 28-33-02' alone produce a substantial positive?

details.result:
Using signed native product, the Colorado C.R.S. condition c1 is strongly positive across all three supplied frames (max products 280.0, 300.0, 246.0). The CO-number-then-C.R.S. condition c2 is positive but much lower (77.5, 68.5, 57.75). The critical non-Colorado condition c3, 'per statutory reference in section 28-33-02', is also substantially positive rather than weak or negative (max products 93.0, 55.5, 87.5; means 29.68, 19.34, 30.02). The other non-Colorado section c4 is similarly positive (162.0, 135.0, 145.0), while the grant-number control c5 is near zero or negative (max products -0.918, -0.551, -0.367). The selected tokens are within the replacement spans, excluding the common prefix. Thus the phrase plus a section-like number alone produces a substantial positive, though explicit C.R.S. material produces a larger positive. This rejects the working hypothesis that a non-Colorado section number in this frame is weak or negative; the rival is supported in direction, with the refinement that Colorado statutory material amplifies rather than being necessary within these supplied frames.
Suggested revision: Refine P2 from a Colorado-marker-required rule to a graded legal-reference citation frame: 'per statutory reference in' plus a section-like number is positive on its own, while explicit C.R.S./Colorado statutory material strongly amplifies the response; grant identifiers remain negative. Next round should test non-legal numeric strings and other legal-reference phrasings to separate section-number formatting from the legal-reference frame.
Evidence: r1-i4-f1-c1, r1-i4-f1-c2, r1-i4-f1-c3, r1-i4-f1-c4, r1-i4-f1-c5, r1-i4-f2-c1, r1-i4-f2-c2, r1-i4-f2-c3, r1-i4-f2-c4, r1-i4-f2-c5, r1-i4-f3-c1, r1-i4-f3-c2, r1-i4-f3-c3, r1-i4-f3-c4, r1-i4-f3-c5

criticism:r1-i5.label: Criticism · r1-i5
criticism:r1-i5.text: Follow-up round 1: Do the strongest non-Colorado positives (Bolivia, Nepal, University at Albany, liberal-democracy, diabetes) share a recurrent frame such as 'state/institution/education/history/research', or are they heterogeneous residuals with no common Colorado-like cue?

details.result:
Comparing both predictions: the rival predicts the listed non-Colorado highs should mostly share a state/institution/education/history/research phrase and resemble Colorado P5. The supplied rows do not show that. spectrum-893937's measured peak is 94.0 on 'Colorado', while earlier University at Albany tokens are near zero ('University' 0.14, 'at' 4.5, 'Albany' 0.71), so it is a Colorado positive, not a non-Colorado residual. spectrum-13884717 likewise contains 'University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus' in the prefix and high Colorado/medical tokens, so diabetes is not a clean non-Colorado case. spectrum-4472100 has cut_left=true, so omitted earlier context prevents classifying liberal-democracy as non-Colorado. The remaining verified non-Colorado rows are heterogeneous: spectrum-12987871 (157.0) is Bolivia political-history prose with high function-word/name activations ('of' 157.0, 'in' 157.0, 'the' 136.0), while spectrum-19807720 (77.0) is Nepal travel/culture with high 'of' 77.0 and 'The' 76.0, not a shared institution/education/history/research phrase. The Colorado P5 comparison search-1-P5-0 (251.0 on 'Atmospheric') shows the actual Colorado higher-education/science frame. Thus the working hypothesis holds only after narrowing: the listed set overcounts non-Colorado positives, and the valid residuals do not support a new broad positive rule; the rival's common frame is not established. Corpus matching remains exploratory and lexical, and these few rows do not establish unbiased prevalence.
Suggested revision: For the next round, label a case non-Colorado only when the measured anchor's causal prefix contains no Colorado token and cut_left is false. Reclassify spectrum-893937 and spectrum-13884717 as Colorado positives; drop or refetch spectrum-4472100 because cut_left=true. Then test a larger balanced full-context set of non-Colorado state/institution/education/history/research positives against Colorado P5, and keep no new broad positive rule unless a recurring expression appears across verified non-Colorado cases.
Evidence: search-1-P5-0, spectrum-12987871, spectrum-13884717, spectrum-19807720, spectrum-4472100, spectrum-893937

criticism:r2-i1.label: Criticism · r2-i1
criticism:r2-i1.text: Follow-up round 2: Does Colorado appearing as one item in a multi-state regional list itself suppress P1 positivity, or are the r1-i1 negative list/admin cases driven by the anchor falling in another jurisdiction's contact/plateau frame while Colorado list/tourism contexts remain positive?

details.result:
Both predictions compared. The working hypothesis predicted positive Colorado-linked multi-state tourism/list contexts and a negative localized to a non-Colorado administrative/contact anchor. Supplied results match: spectrum-76348622 is +165.0 and spectrum-76348696 is +98.0 overall, with high token values on Colorado-linked names (e.g., 'Colorado' +141.0, 'Northwest' +81.0, 'Southwestern' +78.5 in spectrum-76348622; 'Colorado' +141.0, 'North Park' +143.0, 'Continental' +98.0 in spectrum-76348696). Both are cut_left/cut_right and overlap heavily, so they are not independent validation. spectrum-20801103 is overall -22.375, but the peak negative falls on the final non-Colorado phone ')' at -22.375, while the multi-state list token 'Colorado' is +103.0 and 'North Dakota' is -12.3125; the negative is therefore anchor-localized rather than caused by Colorado being one list item. Among refined controls, colorado-name-specificity:refined:0 is +68.5 on 'Colorado', refined:3 Utah is weak at +2.640625, and refined:6 North Dakota is -7.75. The rival predicted weak/negative multi-state list contexts or non-localized list suppression; that is contradicted by the positive spectrum-76348622/spectrum-76348696 contexts and by the +103.0 'Colorado' token inside the negative spectrum-20801103. Verdict: the working hypothesis survived as stated. Limits: cut context on the 763 cases and 20801103, overlapping 763 rows, exploratory lexical matching, and no held-out validation.
Suggested revision: Keep P1 but add an explicit sub-rule for the next round: multi-state list membership alone does not suppress the Colorado named-entity response; suppression requires the measured anchor to fall inside another jurisdiction's contact/admin/citation string or a competing other-jurisdiction institutional/place cue. Test held-out, full-context, balanced multi-state lists and plateau/tourism mentions with Colorado and non-Colorado controls, and do not treat overlapping spectrum-76348622 and spectrum-76348696 as independent validation.
Evidence: spectrum-20801103, spectrum-76348622, spectrum-76348696, colorado-name-specificity:refined:0, colorado-name-specificity:refined:3, colorado-name-specificity:refined:6

criticism:r2-i2.label: Criticism · r2-i2
criticism:r2-i2.text: Follow-up round 2: Does the r1-i4 graded legal-reference-citation effect generalize to natural legal citation/reference prose, or is it specific to the exact 'per statutory reference in' plus section-number construction?

details.result:
Both predictions are only weakly tested. The corpus groups for the exact 'per statutory reference in' construction and for natural Colorado statute citations yielded zero eligible selected documents, so they cannot establish survival. The 12 federal/other-jurisdiction rows are mostly lexical matches on ' code', ' codes', '-coded', or 'encoded' in programming, genetics, area-code, or ordinary prose, with signed products near zero: d33479 -0.1357, d36816 -0.0811, d49051 -0.2021, d96826 -0.0396; none are natural legal-citation positives. Among more citation-like or formatted rows, Pub. L. No. 90-284/82 Stat. 73 (d92356) is only 0.4219, Civil Code (d53875) is -0.1084, and phone identifiers (435) d71164 and (775) d93300 are negative -23.375 and -8.625. The largest selected positive is d60687 at 0.8008 on ' U', but its context is not a clear statutory citation. Thus the rival's substantial positive legal-reference effect is not supported, but the working construction-specific hypothesis also cannot be confirmed because many selected anchors are not legal citations and the relevant exact/Colorado groups had no eligible documents. Exploratory lexical matching limits semantic claims and prevalence.
Suggested revision: For the next round, restrict corpus queries to actual citation syntax (C.R.S., U.S.C., N.D.C.C., Pub. L., Stat., section symbols) and anchor on citation digits or section markers; exclude generic 'code', 'codes', 'encoded', 'area code', and similar lexical controls. Ensure eligible selected documents for the exact 'per statutory reference in [section-like number]' construction and for natural Colorado statute citations, then compare those to natural other-jurisdiction legal citations and to nonlegal identifier controls in full context. Keep P2 construction-specific only if natural legal citations remain weak or near zero once real citations are sampled; do not claim survival from the current lexical corpus matches.

criticism:r2-i3.label: Criticism · r2-i3
criticism:r2-i3.text: Follow-up round 2: Does other-jurisdiction negativity require both an other-jurisdiction name and formal administrative/contact/citation formatting, or does the place name alone suffice after r1-i3's N2 narrowing?

details.result:
The working hypothesis survives and the rival is not supported. In all three frames the full New Mexico administrative block is strongly negative by signed native product (-27.25, -27.0, -29.25), while the New Mexico name alone is weak or positive (-0.820, +6.156, +3.094), and Bismarck, North Dakota alone is only weakly negative (-3.25, -4.125, -2.391), far from the full-block magnitudes. Generic phone controls are near zero or mixed (+1.391, -0.566, +2.563), and generic section controls are positive (+20.5, +18.0, +21.75), so formatting without an other-jurisdiction name is not a negative. Thus strong other-jurisdiction negativity requires the conjunction of an other-jurisdiction name and formal administrative/contact/citation framing in these supplied contrasts; the place name alone does not approach it. Limits: this is one controlled replacement contrast across three synthetic frames, not held-out validation, and it does not establish broad prevalence.
Suggested revision: Refine N2/N4 to require both an other-jurisdiction name and a formal administrative/contact/citation block for strong negativity; treat bare other-jurisdiction place names as weak/mixed rather than reliable negatives, and keep generic section strings from counting as negatives because the supplied generic section controls are positive. Next round should test additional other jurisdictions and held-out full contexts.

criticism:r2-i4.label: Criticism · r2-i4
criticism:r2-i4.text: Follow-up round 2: When Colorado and another jurisdiction's institution appear in the same causal prefix, does the competing institution globally suppress the Colorado frame, or does negativity stay local to the other-jurisdiction token while Colorado tokens remain positive regardless of order?

details.result:
Comparing both predictions, the rival's global-suppression claim is not supported. In spectrum-68446290, Colorado tokens remain strongly positive before the later other-jurisdiction token: ' Colorado' 191, '(' 222, 'B' 241, ' Boulder' 50.25, while negativity is local at ' Dakota' -20.375, '.' -16.25, and 'Grand' -21.625; this is local, not global, suppression, though cut_left means earlier context is unresolved. In spectrum-67930941, earlier East Anglia material is weak or near-neutral (University 0.703, East 0.049, Anglia 0.512/0.777), while the later Colorado frame is strongly positive (University 157, Colorado 177, Atmospheric 270). In spectrum-88026454, earlier ALA/Philadelphia material is weak/neutral (American -0.0016, Library -0.104, Association -0.512, Philadelphia 0.236), while later Colorado Territory/statehood material is strongly positive (Colorado 127.5, 'is' 286, Cent 151, ennial 97.5). The P5 controls are also positive (search-1-P5-1 peak 186 on ' Colorado'; search-2-P5-1 peak 227 on ' Colorado'). Thus Colorado tokens remain positive despite competing other-jurisdiction material before or after them, and negativity, where present, is local. However, the stronger working-hypothesis clause that the competing institution itself carries negative at its own token is not uniform: East Anglia and ALA/Philadelphia are weak or neutral rather than negative. These are reused/generated comparisons, not held-out validation, and cut_left limits full-context claims for spectrum-68446290.
Suggested revision: Retain the local-not-global core: in mixed prefixes, Colorado named-entity tokens can remain strongly positive while any negative stays at a competing other-jurisdiction token, not across the whole Colorado frame. Narrow the negative-local clause so it applies to strong other-jurisdiction named entities or administrative identifiers such as 'North Dakota' rather than every foreign or civic institution; East Anglia and ALA/Philadelphia were weak/neutral in the supplied evidence. Next round should test held-out mixed contexts in both orders with full causal prefixes, and should not treat a merely neutral other-jurisdiction mention as evidence of local negativity.
Evidence: spectrum-68446290, spectrum-67930941, spectrum-88026454, search-1-P5-1, search-2-P5-1

criticism:r2-i5.label: Criticism · r2-i5
criticism:r2-i5.text: Follow-up round 2: Do verified non-Colorado place contexts show broad country-name negativity, or does polarity vary by surrounding frame across Bolivia, Nepal, and Bhutan such that neither a broad place-name rule nor a new positive rule is warranted?

details.result:
Using signed native product, the rival broad country-name negativity prediction fails. All 12 Bolivia-group rows are positive (products 5.0 to 89.0; e.g., corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d3771 41.75, g1-d84766 89.0, g1-d82360 62.5, g1-d37342 29.125). The Nepal group is also positive or near zero: actual Nepal/demonym rows are positive (g2-d51383 28.0, g2-d70731 22.0, g2-d89474 18.25, g2-d21939 15.3125, g2-d9538 11.5, g2-d97620 10.75, g2-d57083 7.625, g2-d31321 12.1875, g2-d60122 10.25), and no strongly negative Nepal row appears; 'Newark' substring matches are near zero (g2-d22793 0.042, g2-d26128 -0.122, g2-d83887 -0.043). By contrast, the Bhutan-specific negative part is not verified: the negative Bhutan-group anchors are weak and mostly on non-Bhutan substrings or false lexical matches (g3-d15877 -0.906, g3-d34858 -0.430, g3-d66026 -0.418, g3-d67360 -0.301, g3-d84078 -0.275, g3-d86386 -0.119, g3-d90591 -0.084), while the ' Bh' anchors are positive (g3-d35846 7.031, g3-d57811 5.594) and only put 'Bh' in the causal prefix, not full 'Bhutan'. Controls are mixed and mostly weak: Texas/California near zero or weak (g4-d9579 0.178, g4-d13017 -1.203, g4-d3787 -0.266, g4-d13930 -0.680, g4-d40276 -0.103, g4-d65025 0.053, g4-d76154 0.197), Utah/Montana positive (g4-d24756 5.3125, g4-d70969 8.625), Qinghai/North Dakota more negative (g4-d34737 -11.875, g4-d42988 -11.5625). Thus broad non-Colorado country/place negativity is rejected, and no new broad positive rule is established; the working hypothesis survives only as a narrowed claim that polarity is not country-name-wide, but the specific Bhutan conservation/natural-heritage negative prediction needs full-token causal-prefix verification. Corpus matching is exploratory and lexical; these rows include substring false positives and cannot establish semantic coverage or unbiased prevalence.
Suggested revision: Retain withdrawal of broad non-Colorado place-name negativity. Drop or refine the Bhutan conservation/natural-heritage negative subclaim until full literal 'Bhutan'/'Bhutanese' tokens are in causal_prefix and cut_left=false; require full-token country/demonym anchors and exclude substring matches like 'Gasa' in Nagasaki, 'Newar' in Newark, and 'Paro' in parodies. Test a balanced full-context Bolivia/Nepal/Bhutan and control set, and do not add a broad positive rule unless a recurring full-token frame is observed. Request full-context review where only 'Bh' is available in the causal prefix.
Evidence: corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d3771, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d23040, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d23930, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d31249, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d37342, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d52106, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d69182, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d71359, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d82360, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d83787, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d84766, corpus-d2d87310b966-g1-d93603, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d9538, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d21939, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d22793, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d26128, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d31321, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d51383, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d57083, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d60122, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d70731, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d83887, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d89474, corpus-d2d87310b966-g2-d97620, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d15877, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d34858, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d35846, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d44454, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d57811, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d66026, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d67360, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d82944, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d84078, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d86386, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d90591, corpus-d2d87310b966-g3-d92955, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d13017, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d13930, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d24756, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d34737, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d3787, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d40076, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d40276, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d42988, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d65025, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d70969, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d76154, corpus-d2d87310b966-g4-d9579

original_criticism.prediction: Bolivia, Nepal, Texas, Utah and New Mexico place contexts should be consistently strongly negative.
original_criticism.result: The broad place-name account fails. The frozen P1 family was 84/87 positive, yet its three misses were Colorado-list or Colorado-plateau contexts scored negative (20801103, 64969991, 51093128). Controls put California, Texas, Utah, New Mexico and a country near neutral, with Nevada -7.34, North Dakota -7.75, and Qinghai -4.65, not uniformly strong. Non-Colorado positives remain, so the broad negative rule is rejected rather than confirmed.

original_criticism.attack: Explicit Colorado name is sufficient for positivity.
original_criticism.prediction: Any explicit Colorado name before the anchor should be strongly positive unless only continuation after the anchor.
original_criticism.result: Explicit Colorado is usually positive but not sufficient. P1 is 84/87 positive, and P5 is 31/32, yet P1 has negative Colorado-list and Colorado-Plateau cases, and P5 includes 68446290, where a University of Colorado list precedes a North Dakota anchor and the measured value is -20.375. The rule should be narrowed by competing other-jurisdiction administrative framing and list context, not treated as a context-free Colorado keyword detector.

original_criticism.attack: N2 catches all other-jurisdiction contact strings.
original_criticism.prediction: Other-jurisdiction contact strings should be negative regardless of local institutional or clinic context.
original_criticism.result: N2 is strong but not jurisdiction-general. It is 33/35 negative and N4 is 17/17 negative, mostly on North Dakota 701, N.D.C.C., Nevada 775, Utah 435, and Qinghai grants. However, 56828588 (Montana 406 contact) and 53716305 (Utah foot clinics 801) are measured positive. These are ordinary local institutional/contact contexts, so N2 should be narrowed to formatted administrative/citation/grant blocks, leaving other-jurisdiction clinic or civic contacts as unresolved counterexamples.

original_criticism.attack: Generic citation, digit or punctuation formatting.
original_criticism.prediction: Bare section symbols, digits, or grant numbers should be positive by format alone.
original_criticism.result: The generic-citation rival fails. P2 is only 3/3 positive, but its controls separate frames: C.R.S. prefix 280, C.R.S. suffix 79.5 and section-symbol form 304, while bare digits peak at 20 and a grant number is -0.957. N.D.C.C. § 28-33-02 is -28 and the Qinghai grant block is -38.25. Citation punctuation alone is therefore rejected; Colorado statutory material is doing the work, though P2's tiny sample limits generalization.

plan.reason: The original criticism leaves specific causal-prefix questions unresolved: whether the P1 misses actually had explicit Colorado in the causal prefix, whether the 68446290 negative is driven by a competing other-jurisdiction administrative frame rather than Colorado/list context, whether the N2 counterexamples fall outside the formatted-admin causal-prefix scope, whether P2 is truly Colorado-specific or partly a generic 'per statutory reference' legal frame, and whether strong non-Colorado positives share any recurring positive frame. These are distinct and can change the frozen interpretation.

Controls are mixed and mostly weak: Texas/California near zero or weak (g4-d9579 0.178, g4-d13017 -1.203, g4-d3787 -0.266, g4-d13930 -0.680, g4-d40276 -0.103, g4-d65025 0.053, g4-d76154 0.197), Utah/Montana positive (g4-d24756 5.3125, g4-d70969 8.625), Qinghai/North Dakota more negative (g4-d34737 -11.875, g4-d42988 -11.5625). Thus broad non-Colorado country/place negativity is rejected, and no new broad positive rule is established; the working hypothesis survives only as a narrowed claim that polarity is not country-name-wide, but the specific Bhutan conservation/natural-heritage negative prediction needs full-token causal-prefix verification. Corpus matching is exploratory and lexical; these rows include substring false positives and cannot establish semantic coverage or unbiased prevalence.

claim.title: Colorado named-entity/jurisdiction frame with narrow other-jurisdiction administrative suppression
claim.lede: The neuron is primarily a Colorado named-entity and jurisdiction detector. Strong positives occur on explicit Colorado or Colorado-derived names, Colorado institutions/places, C.R.S. citations, Colorado area codes/URLs/local media, and Colorado statehood/history or higher-education/science frames, often on a nearby space or function word in the causal prefix. The negative pole is much narrower than earlier: broad non-Colorado place-name and measurement rules were withdrawn because many such contexts are positive or weak. Reliable negatives are other-jurisdiction administrative/contact/citation strings; negative coverage is sparse.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: I would restore a non-Colorado place-name negative rule if many non-Colorado place contexts, including Bolivia, Nepal, Texas, Utah, and New Mexico, were consistently strongly negative rather than positive or weak. I would withdraw Colorado specificity if explicit Colorado names in the causal prefix were often weak or negative without an intervening factor. I would revise the administrative-negative rules if 701/775/435, N.D.C.C., or Qinghai grant strings were often strong positive. I would add a new positive rule if strong non-Colorado positives clustered around a nameable recurring expression; currently they remain unresolved. Tiny near-zero sign flips alone should not overturn the supported patterns.
claim.one_paragraph: Positive when the prefix before the marked position contains 'Colorado' or a Colorado-built name ('state of Colorado', 'University of Colorado', 'Colorado State University', 'Colorado School of Public Health', 'Colorado Department of ...', 'Colorado Women's Education Foundation', 'Colorado Labor Wars') or a Colorado-linked place/institution ('Denver', 'Boulder', 'Arvada', 'Longmont', 'Aspen', 'Pueblo', 'Rocky Mountain' in a Colorado frame). The high value may sit on an adjacent space or function word inside that name. The cue must be in the causal prefix; continuation after the anchor (e.g. 'Colorado Plateaus' after 'within') does not count. Non-Colorado names do not by themselves establish a negative response. Positive on the Colorado statutory citation pattern '§ 22-5-119, C.R.S.', '22-5-199, C.R.S.' or 'per statutory reference in [number]' within Colorado blended-learning or state-law material. High values can fall on spaces, digits, section symbols, hyphens, or punctuation inside or immediately before the citation. The same punctuation and digits without the Colorado statute frame do not suffice; N.D.C.C. or Qinghai grant numbers are not positive by format alone. Positive when a Colorado entity/address/local-media frame is present: Denver 303/720/970 numbers such as 720-848-18..., 'Longmont, CO', '.co.us', 'colostate.edu', or '9NEWS'. The high value may be on the space, slash, digit, or adjacent ordinary token. Area code, phone punctuation, or URL form alone is not a cue; analogous 701/775/435 strings in other-jurisdiction administrative material are not positive. Positive in Colorado state-history frames: 'Colorado became the thirty-eighth state', 'Its nickname is the Centennial State', 'Colorado became a state on August 1, 1876', and 'Colorado Labor Wars, 1903-1904'. The response can land on 'is' before the nickname or a space before the date. Parallel statehood or history facts for other states are not enough; they are not negative by topic alone. Positive around Colorado-linked universities, research, and local news: CU Boulder, University of Colorado, Colorado State University, Colorado School of Public Health, Denver Museum of Nature & Science, NOAA/NCAR in Boulder, CSU Extension, and 9NEWS. High values can appear on 'University', 'State', 'Public', 'Atmospheric', 'Boulder', 'Denver', or nearby spaces/digits only within such a frame. The bare generic word outside a Colorado frame is not reliable.
claim.negative_pole: Negative on contact, citation, or grant strings tied to another jurisdiction in the prefix: North Dakota '(701) 328-1504' or a 701 phone in Game and Fish CWD material, N.D.C.C. '§ 28-33-02' with hyphens and digits, Nevada/Utah 775/435 phone strings, or Qinghai grant 'No. 11761056' with parentheses and digits. The cue is the other-jurisdiction administrative/identifier frame, often involving punctuation and digits; generic numbers, punctuation, or a non-Colorado place name alone are not reliable negatives. Negative on legal or administrative boilerplate for another jurisdiction: North Dakota Department of Agriculture/IPM address-phone block, North Dakota Game and Fish CWD contact, N.D.C.C. citations, and New Mexico or Qinghai grant/address material. This rule does not suppress ordinary discussion of other states or regions, which can be positive or weak; it targets formatted other-jurisdiction administrative and legal identifiers.

proposed_revisions.revision: Refine P1 so that explicit 'Colorado' in the causal prefix is necessary but not sufficient: exclude cases where the anchor is inside another jurisdiction's contact/citation/admin string or where Colorado appears only as one item in a multi-state regional list or as a plateau/geologic term. Treat spectrum-20801103, spectrum-64969991, and spectrum-51093128 as counterexamples requiring that narrowing.

Refine P5/N2 for the next round: keep Colorado higher-education/list frames positive when the causal prefix remains Colorado-framed, but add a narrow exception for a later competing other-jurisdiction institutional/place named entity in the same prefix (e.g., 'University of North Dakota'/'North Dakota') that can carry the negative at that later anchor. Do not generalize this to non-Colorado place names alone; require a competing institutional/place frame and test it on held-out contexts.

Narrow N2 to formal other-jurisdiction administrative, legal, citation, or grant blocks in the causal prefix, with anchor-local punctuation/digit evidence, and do not treat ordinary clinic/civic contact pages as covered unless the anchor is on a formal administrative/citation string. Treat spectrum-56828588 and spectrum-53716305 as unresolved ordinary-contact/civic-contact exceptions rather than as support for a broad 'any other-jurisdiction contact string' rule; keep spectrum-13854828 as a boundary case showing that some ordinary civic contact blocks can still be negative.

Refine P2 from a Colorado-marker-required rule to a graded legal-reference citation frame: 'per statutory reference in' plus a section-like number is positive on its own, while explicit C.R.S./Colorado statutory material strongly amplifies the response; grant identifiers remain negative. Next round should test non-legal numeric strings and other legal-reference phrasings to separate section-number formatting from the legal-reference frame.

For the next round, label a case non-Colorado only when the measured anchor's causal prefix contains no Colorado token and cut_left is false. Reclassify spectrum-893937 and spectrum-13884717 as Colorado positives; drop or refetch spectrum-4472100 because cut_left=true. Then test a larger balanced full-context set of non-Colorado state/institution/education/history/research positives against Colorado P5, and keep no new broad positive rule unless a recurring expression appears across verified non-Colorado cases.

Keep P1 but add an explicit sub-rule for the next round: multi-state list membership alone does not suppress the Colorado named-entity response; suppression requires the measured anchor to fall inside another jurisdiction's contact/admin/citation string or a competing other-jurisdiction institutional/place cue. Test held-out, full-context, balanced multi-state lists and plateau/tourism mentions with Colorado and non-Colorado controls, and do not treat overlapping spectrum-76348622 and spectrum-76348696 as independent validation.

For the next round, restrict corpus queries to actual citation syntax (C.R.S., U.S.C., N.D.C.C., Pub. L., Stat., section symbols) and anchor on citation digits or section markers; exclude generic 'code', 'codes', 'encoded', 'area code', and similar lexical controls. Ensure eligible selected documents for the exact 'per statutory reference in [section-like number]' construction and for natural Colorado statute citations, then compare those to natural other-jurisdiction legal citations and to nonlegal identifier controls in full context. Keep P2 construction-specific only if natural legal citations remain weak or near zero once real citations are sampled; do not claim survival from the current lexical corpus matches.

Refine N2/N4 to require both an other-jurisdiction name and a formal administrative/contact/citation block for strong negativity; treat bare other-jurisdiction place names as weak/mixed rather than reliable negatives, and keep generic section strings from counting as negatives because the supplied generic section controls are positive.
